elements.text: Form: f(x) = b^x where b > 0 and b != 1

segments.speech: An exponential function has a variable in the exponent, like f(x) equals b to the x power. Think of it like population growth or money compounding in a bank account—it starts slow, then shoots up really fast! Does that curve make sense so far?

elements.text: Let's say bacteria double every hour. Start with 1 bacterium at x = 0.
At x=3 hours, we get 2^3 = 8 bacteria!

segments.speech: Let's look at a concrete example, Roosevelt. Imagine a population of bacteria that doubles every single hour. If we start with just one bacterium, our function is f of x equals two to the x power. After three hours, x is three, so two cubed gives us eight bacteria. Does doubling make sense so far?

elements.text: Notice how the curve rises steeply as x increases. It never touches the x-axis, creating a horizontal asymptote.

segments.speech: Notice how the graph shoots up rapidly, Roosevelt? It gets closer and closer to zero on the left, but never touches it. That flat boundary line is called an asymptote. Does that visual make sense to you?
